questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Factorial in an Equivalent Form
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $(n+3)!$ for any $n\ge -1?$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the definition of factorial, we have

$$
(n+3)!=(n+3)\cdot (n+2)\cdot (n+1)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1.
$$

Now, applying the factorial definition to all but the first factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(n+3)! & =(n+3)\cdot \overset{(n+2)!}{\overset{⏞}{(n+2)\cdot (n+1)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =(n+3)\cdot (n+2)!\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Variable Expression Containing a Quotient of Factorials
questions.problem: Given that $n\ge 1$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(n+1)!}{(n-1)!}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice the following:

$$
(n+1)!=(n+1)\cdot n\cdot (n-1)!
$$

Then, we cancel the $(n-1)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n+1)!}{(n-1)!} & =\frac{(n+1)\cdot n\cdot (n-1)!}{(n-1)!} \\  & =\frac{(n+1)\cdot n\cdot \cancel{(n-1)!}}{\cancel{(n-1)!}} \\  & =n(n+1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $k\ge 0$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(k+3)!}{(k+1)k!}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice the following:

$$
(k+3)!=(k+3)\cdot (k+2)\cdot (k+1)\cdot k!
$$

Then, we cancel the $k!$ and $(k+1)$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(k+3)!}{(k+1)k!}= & \frac{(k+3)\cdot (k+2)\cdot (k+1)\cdot k!}{(k+1)\cdot k!} \\ = & \frac{(k+3)\cdot (k+2)\cdot \cancel{(k+1)}\cdot \cancel{k!}}{\cancel{(k+1)}\cdot \cancel{k!}} \\ = & (k+3)(k+2) \\ = & {k}^{2}+5k+6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $n\ge -1$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(n+1)!}{(n+2)!}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice the following:

$$
(n+2)!=(n+2)\cdot (n+1)!
$$

Then, we cancel the $(n+1)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n+1)!}{(n+2)!} & =\frac{(n+1)!}{(n+2)\cdot (n+1)!} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(n+1)!}}{(n+2)\cdot \cancel{(n+1)!}} \\  & =\frac{1}{n+2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $n\ge 2$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(n-1)^{2}\,(n-1)!}{(n-2)!}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}(n-1)! & =(n-1)(n-2)!\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can cancel the $(n-2)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n-1)^{2}\cdot (n-1)!}{(n-2)!} & =\frac{(n-1)^{2}\cdot (n-1)\cdot (n-2)!}{(n-2)!} \\  & =\frac{(n-1)^{2}\cdot (n-1)\cancel{(n-2)!}}{\cancel{(n-2)!}} \\  & =(n-1)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $n\ge -3$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(n+6)!}{(n+5)\text{ }(n+3)!}=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we notice that

$$
(n+6)!=(n+6)(n+5)(n+4)(n+3)!
$$

Then, we can cancel the $(n+5)$ and $(n+3)!$ that occur in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n+6)!}{(n+5)\text{ }(n+3)!} & =\frac{(n+6)\cdot (n+5)\cdot (n+4)\cdot (n+3)!}{(n+5)\cdot (n+3)!} \\  & =\frac{(n+6)\cdot \cancel{(n+5)}\cdot (n+4)\cdot \cancel{(n+3)!}}{\cancel{(n+5)}\cdot \cancel{(n+3)!}} \\  & =(n+6)\cdot (n+4) \\  & ={n}^{2}+10n+24\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $n\ge 9$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(n-8)!\,(n+9)!}{(n-9)!\,(n+7)!}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}(n+9)! & =(n+9)(n+8)(n+7)! \\ (n-8)! & =(n-8)(n-9)!\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can cancel the $(n+7)!$ and $(n-9)!$ that occur in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n-8)!\,(n+9)!}{(n-9)!\,(n+7)!} & =\frac{[(n-8)\cdot (n-9)!]\cdot [(n+9)\cdot (n+8)\cdot (n+7)!]}{(n-9)!\cdot (n+7)!} \\  & =\frac{(n-8)\cdot \cancel{(n-9)!}\cdot (n+9)\cdot (n+8)\cdot \cancel{(n+7)!}}{\cancel{(n-9)!}\cdot \cancel{(n+7)!}} \\  & =(n-8)\cdot (n+8)\cdot (n+9) \\  & =(n-8)(n+8)(n+9)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Writing a Factorial in an Equivalent Form
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $(k+1)!$ for any $k \geq 2?$

- $(k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1)$

- $(k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1)!$

- $(k+1) \cdot k$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the definition of factorial, we have 

$$
(k+1)! = (k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1) \cdot (k-2) \cdot \: \cdots \: \cdot 2 \cdot 1.
$$

Now, applying the factorial definition to all but the first two factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k+1)! & =(k+1)\cdot k\cdot \overset{(k-1)!}{\overset{⏞}{(k-1)\cdot (k-2)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =(k+1)\cdot k\cdot (k-1)!\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Variable Expression Containing a Quotient of Factorials
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $n \geq 2$ is an integer, simplify $\dfrac {n!} {(n - 2)!}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice the following:

$$
n! = n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2)!
$$

Then, we cancel the $(n-2)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac {n!} {(n - 2)!} 
&= \dfrac {n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2)!} {(n - 2)!}\[5pt] 

&= \dfrac {n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot \cancel{(n - 2)!}} {\cancel{(n - 2)!}}\[5pt] 

&= n(n -1) \[5pt]
&= n^2 - n
	}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Variable Expression Containing a Quotient With Many Factorials
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $k \geq 1$ is an integer, simplify $\dfrac {k^2(k - 1)!} {k!}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we notice that 

$$
k! = k \cdot (k-1)!
$$

So, we can simplify the numerator as follows:

$$
k^2 (k-1)! = k \cdot \underbrace{k \cdot (k-1)!}_{k!} = k \cdot k!
$$

Then, we cancel the $k!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac {k^2(k - 1)!} {k!} 
&= \dfrac {k \cdot k!} {k!}\[5pt]
&= \dfrac {k \cdot \cancel{k!}} {\cancel{k!}} \[5pt]
&= \dfrac {k} {1} \[5pt]
&= k
	}
$$
